desc:
You begin with start units of money. In each round you win one unit with probability a / (a + b) and lose one unit otherwise. You stop when your money reaches 0 (ruin) or target (success).

Find the probability of reaching target before 0, as a reduced fraction p/q with no spaces.

a = 1, b = 1, start = 1, target = 4 -> 1/4
a = 1, b = 2, start = 1, target = 2 -> 1/3
a = 1, b = 1, start = 0, target = 5 -> 0/1
hints: Let P(i) be the success probability from money i. It satisfies P(i) = p * P(i + 1) + q * P(i - 1) with P(0) = 0 and P(target) = 1, where p = a / (a + b) and q = b / (a + b).
Let r = q / p = b / a. The equation becomes P(i + 1) - P(i) = r * (P(i) - P(i - 1)), so the differences form a geometric sequence. Summing them gives P(i) = (1 - ri) / (1 - rtarget).
When a = b then r = 1 and the answer is simply start / target. Use fractions.Fraction so the arithmetic stays exact.
editorial: Condition on the first round. With probability p you move up one unit and with probability q you move down one, so P(i) = p P(i + 1) + q P(i - 1) for 0 < i < target, with boundary values P(0) = 0 and P(target) = 1.

Write r = q / p = b / a. Rearranging gives P(i + 1) - P(i) = r * (P(i) - P(i - 1)). So each step is r times the previous one, and the first step P(1) - P(0) = P(1) sets the scale. Summing the geometric series from 0 to start - 1 and using P(target) = 1 to fix the scale gives P(start) = (1 - rstart) / (1 - rtarget) when r differs from 1, and start / target when it equals 1.

The exact fraction can have around 57 digits in the numerator and denominator for the largest inputs. Python's Fraction keeps everything exact, so no rounding error can change the reduced answer. The brute-force check solves the linear system for P by Gaussian elimination instead, so it does not rely on the closed form.
